architecture_decisions.recommendation: Created a separate presigned URL generation endpoint instead of embedding file upload in resource creation/update endpoints
architecture_decisions.rationale: Separating URL generation from resource creation follows the single responsibility principle. The client first gets a signed URL, uploads directly to storage, then calls the resource API with just the storage key. This reduces server load, prevents base64 encoding overhead, and enables better error handling for upload failures.
alternatives_considered: Keeping base64 file upload in existing endpoints with size validation
Using multipart form uploads to the same endpoints

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Changed from storing base64-encoded files to storing storage keys and derived URLs
architecture_decisions.rationale: Instead of embedding file data in API requests, the system now stores cloud storage keys (e.g., 'programs/{programId}/logos/...') and constructs URLs server-side using R2_URL. This reduces database bloat, improves performance, and aligns with cloud-native storage patterns. File size validation happens before URL generation.
alternatives_considered: Storing full URLs directly from client uploads

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Implemented comprehensive error handling with user-friendly toast messages and server-side validation
architecture_decisions.rationale: Added try-catch blocks in UI components to catch upload errors and display meaningful messages. Server-side validation includes file size limits (10MB), key path validation, and proper error propagation. Old file deletion happens only after successful database updates to prevent data loss.
alternatives_considered: Generic error messages without specific details

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Added server-side validation of storage key paths and file size limits before URL generation
architecture_decisions.rationale: Prevents path traversal attacks by validating that keys start with 'programs/{programId}/'. Enforces 10MB file size limit server-side before generating signed URLs. Uses short-lived signed URLs (5 minutes) to minimize exposure. Content-Type headers are set appropriately for SVG files.

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Created a custom React hook (useUploadProgramResource) to encapsulate upload logic
architecture_decisions.rationale: Centralizes upload logic including getting signed URLs, setting appropriate headers, and handling the PUT request. Promotes code reuse between logo and file uploads. Provides a clean abstraction that components can consume without dealing with fetch details.
alternatives_considered: Duplicate upload logic in each modal component

architecture_decisions.recommendation: Enhanced storage client to support content-length headers in signed URLs
architecture_decisions.rationale: Added content-length header support to the getSignedUploadUrl method to enforce file size limits at the storage layer. This provides defense in depth - both server validation and storage layer enforcement. The storage client remains generic for reuse across the codebase.
alternatives_considered: Creating a specialized program resource storage client
Hardcoding headers in the UI layer

implementation_summary:
The implementation introduces a client-side upload flow for program brand assets using presigned PUT URLs, replacing the previous base64-embedded file approach. The architecture follows a three-step process: 1) Client requests a signed URL from a new server endpoint with file metadata, 2) Client uploads directly to cloud storage using the signed URL, 3) Client calls existing resource APIs with just the storage key.

Key patterns include separation of concerns between URL generation and resource management, server-side validation before URL issuance, and atomic updates with proper cleanup of old files. The storage client was enhanced to support content-length headers for additional security. A custom React hook encapsulates the upload logic, promoting reuse across logo and file upload components.

The changes integrate well with the existing codebase by maintaining the same API contracts for resource creation/update (with key instead of file), leveraging the existing storage abstraction, and preserving all existing validation and permission checks. The approach reduces server load, improves upload performance for large files, and provides better user feedback during uploads.
